MiniMax's technology export registration covers some recently released and soon-to-be-released models, spanning both open-source release and overseas licensing. The move follows the October 16 public consultation by China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology on a revision to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export, which proposes adding 23 AI technologies to export controls. highlights.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English ![OpenAI and Anthropic slash LLM prices up to 80% as open-weight competition intensifies](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fopenai-and-anthropic-slash-llm-prices-up-to-80-as-open-weight-competition-intensifies-1_1792973724140-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #LLMs # OpenAI and Anthropic slash LLM prices up to 80% as open-weight competition intensifies • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •3 min read Share this article A rapid series of price cuts from both companies since June has driven API costs down 75% or more, driven by competition from open-weight models on platforms like OpenRouter and looming IPO pressures. OpenAI and Anthropic have cut prices for their flagship large language models by as much as 80% over the past four months, a pace of decline that has surprised even close observers of the AI market. The reductions coincide with a flood of open-weight models from competitors such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, which are now served by dozens of inference providers on routing platforms like OpenRouter. The price war began in late June when OpenAI released GPT-5.6 Luna at $1 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens. By July 30, OpenAI had slashed Luna's price 80% to $0.20 and $1.20 respectively. Anthropic followed in August by making a temporary launch discount for Claude Sonnet 5 permanent, then cut Opus 5.5 pricing 40-60% in September. OpenAI responded days later with GPT-6.1 Sol at half the input and output cost of its predecessor and a cache-read price matching Anthropic's at 5% of input cost. "Starting from the release of the GPT-5.6 model families in June to now, the cost of using these popular LLMs has cratered, which is not something I would have expected a year ago," wrote Max Woolf, a former senior data scientist at BuzzFeed who tracks model pricing on his blog. Cache-read costs matter disproportionately for agentic coding workflows, where the conversation history is cached and re-read each turn. Those reads account for 96-99% of total token spend. A 75% reduction in cache-read pricing translates to a 70-75% drop in effective cost for developers using tools like Codex and Claude Code. Data from Vercel's AI model gateway shows cost-per-token falling to 43.3% of April 2026 levels, though aggregate spend continues to rise as models improve faster than they cheapen. The competitive pressure extends beyond the two labs. DeepSeek's Flash V4.1 1017 variant, released in April at $0.15/$0.60/$0.003, is now hosted by 29 distinct inference providers on OpenRouter, up from 13 in May. Providers including Cloudflare and DeepInfra offer effective costs within 10% of DeepSeek's own endpoint. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.1 Pro, slated for weight release November 4, matches Opus 5.5 performance at half the input/output price. "OpenAI and Anthropic will have to differentiate from these open weight models with higher-quality models—they are currently doing a good job with that particularly with Opus 5.5—but they need to keep doing that," Woolf wrote. The timing raises questions about upcoming public offerings. OpenAI is rumored to target a 2027 IPO; Anthropic may file within months. Both companies report billions in losses from R&D and scaling, though those figures predate the recent surge in agentic usage. Cutting the primary revenue line by 80% runs counter to typical pre-IPO positioning, unless inference margins remain healthy—some reports suggest 80% profit-per-token before the latest cuts. Woolf noted the cuts changed his own behavior: after GPT-6.1 Sol reduced effective cost 75%, he lowered his Codex usage quota to one-fifth, keeping spend roughly flat. OpenAI simultaneously cut the $200/month Codex tier's allowance by 50%, citing "increasingly efficient models." The title, Open Source Models and the AI Challenge, is handwritten on either side of the tree.](https://www.bananaip.com/intellepedia/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/open-source-ai-tree-featured-title-1024x239.png) Featured image for: Open Source Models and the AI Challenge *Authors: Kalyan C. Kankanala, BananaIP Counsels; and Anil B. Suraj, IIM, Bangalore.* ## Introduction Open source software is today an integral part of almost all businesses, which use it in one way or another, either directly or through the software and services they buy from others (Kshetri, 2025; White et al., 2024). It is estimated that more than 78% of businesses rely on open source software in their daily operations, and it is used by 90% of Fortune Global 500 companies (Kshetri, 2025). One report states that open source was present in 98% of the 947 commercial codebases that were audited between November 2024 and October 2025 (Black Duck, 2026). Broadly, open source software is based on the principle that the source code of software must be made available for anyone to use, study, modify, and share (Ramos and Pianese, 2026). This is normally accomplished through open source licences, which make the source code available and permit use, study, modification, and distribution, including for commercial purposes, without discriminating against persons or fields of activity (Open Source Initiative, 2024a). Open source licences are broadly of two types, permissive licences and copyleft licences. Permissive licences, such as the MIT and Apache 2.0 licences, give users freedom to use, modify, and distribute the software, with minimum conditions, mainly relating to retention of copyright and licence notices (Kshetri, 2025). Copyleft licences, such as the GNU General Public License, require that original and modified works, when distributed, be also shared under the same licence, so that the source code remains available (Kshetri, 2025). Over the years, the open source model has also moved beyond software into other areas of research, development, and industry. It has been used to share an open standard for designing computer chips (RISC-V International, n.d.), designs of data centre hardware (Open Compute Project, n.d.), biological materials such as DNA (Kahl et al., 2018), and the data and results of drug discovery research (Årdal and Røttingen, 2012; Boby et al., 2023). Open source-like models have also been applied to research infrastructure through which computing power, data storage, and repositories have been shared with researchers (Linåker et al., 2026; Zenodo, n.d.). While open source software has been hugely successful, and a large portion of software is developed through this model, applying open source principles to AI technology has given rise to certain complications (Maffulli, 2025; Widder, Whittaker and West, 2024). Though AI may also be considered as primarily software-based (Ramos and Pianese, 2026), it has several aspects, components, or parts that pose difficulties in applying the open source model to it (Liesenfeld and Dingemanse, 2024). Having said that, there are compelling reasons to make AI open. AI systems that are based on open source can be checked by a wider community for errors and bias, and problems in them can be found and fixed by that community, though this may depend on access to expertise and resources (Dey, 2025). Openness can also help research to be reproduced and built upon (Maffulli, 2025), and it can lower the cost of access for researchers, smaller organisations, and developing countries, which in turn promotes compet...

highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Fine-Tune an LLM With QLoRA: 12 Steps, 90 Min [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 25, 2026 · 35 min read You can fine-tune an LLM on a single consumer GPU in an afternoon, then run the result on your own machine through Ollama. The recipe is QLoRA: freeze a 4-bit copy of the base model, train small low-rank adapter matrices on top, merge the adapter, and export a GGUF file. The practical target here is a support-ticket triage model that returns strict JSON, trained on a synthetic dataset your own script generates in seconds. The [2023 QLoRA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314) from Tim Dettmers and coauthors made the core claim plainly: the method “reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance.” Three years later the base models have changed, but the recipe has held up. What changed is the tooling around it, and that is where most readers get stuck. The stack moved fast this fall. Hugging Face’s latest TRL release is v1.16.0. PEFT v0.21.2 landed on October 1. Ollama v0.40.11 is the current release as of October 24. On the model side, Qwen3.8-27B, a dense, native vision-language model from Alibaba, is the newest 27B-class open-weight checkpoint covered here. If you only want inference on a big card, the walkthrough on [running LLMs locally on an RTX 5090](https://shattered.io/run-llm-locally-rtx-5090/) covers the serving half. What follows covers the training half, end to end. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Why Fine-Tune an LLM Instead of Prompting or RAG Most teams reach for fine-tuning too early. A good system prompt plus a few examples solves a large share of formatting problems, and retrieval-augmented generation handles anything that depends on fresh or private documents. So the first question is not how to fine tune LLM weights. It is whether you need to touch the weights at all. Fine-tuning earns its cost in four situations. The first is a rigid output format that the base model breaks even with careful prompting, such as strict JSON that a downstream parser consumes. The second is a narrow classification or extraction task where you have hundreds of labeled examples and want a small, cheap model to match a large one. The third is a house style or tone that a prompt cannot hold across thousands of calls. The fourth is latency and cost: a tuned model needs a short prompt, because the behavior lives in the weights instead of in 800 tokens of instructions you pay for on every request. It is the wrong tool for teaching a model new facts. Adapters shift behavior, and they absorb knowledge poorly and unreliably. If your goal is answering questions about a changing knowledge base, build retrieval and leave the weights alone. If you need both, tune for format and behavior, then add retrieval for facts. The two approaches stack cleanly. Open-weight models also make the economics different from two years ago. A ranking such as the one in the [best open source LLM roundup](https://shattered.io/best-open-source-llm-october-2026-kimi-glm-deepseek/) shows how many capable checkpoints now exist, and several of them ship under permissive licenses. That means you can tune, merge, and redistribute inside your company without negotiating an API contract. It also means you own the privacy story, since the training data never leaves your machine. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # TorchTPU Goes Open Source: 4 Repos, Oct. 20 [2026] ![Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/lbennett.webp) [Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/author/lbennett/) Updated Oct 26, 2026 · 16 min read Google and Meta open-sourced TorchTPU on October 20, 2026, giving PyTorch developers a native backend for Google TPUs. According to [Google Cloud’s announcement](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/ai-infrastructure/torchtpu-is-now-open-source-run-native-pytorch-on-tpus), the project lets TPUs join GPUs and CPUs as a native option for PyTorch. The reveal came at PyTorch Conference North America 2026 in San Jose, which ran October 20 to 21. The pitch is simple. Take a PyTorch workload you already run, point it at a TPU, and change as little code as you can. For years that promise sat behind a translation layer or a rewrite into another framework. TorchTPU tries to remove that tax, and it does so with Meta’s PyTorch team as a co-developer rather than a bystander. If you already serve models with vLLM, as in our [walkthrough for running an LLM on DGX Spark](https://shattered.io/run-llm-dgx-spark-ollama-vllm-12-steps-2026/), the new repositories suggest the same engine can now target a second kind of silicon. This analysis covers what shipped, what the sources confirm, what stays unproven, and what the release means for CUDA, JAX and the cloud accelerator market. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Google and Meta Announced at PyTorch Conference North America 2026 TorchTPU is an open-source collaboration between Google and Meta. It provides a native PyTorch backend for Google’s Tensor Processing Units. Google Cloud and InfoQ both report the announcement date as October 20, 2026, and the official event pages place the conference in San Jose, California. One naming detail deserves a correction. Many headlines say “PyTorch Conference 2026,” but the official event pages call it PyTorch Conference North America 2026. The distinction matters because the PyTorch community runs regional events, and a reader searching for session videos or slides needs the exact name. Two people introduced the project on stage. Bill Jia of Google Cloud and Zongwei Zhou, a Meta software engineer, presented TorchTPU alongside a segment on agentic developer workflows. The PyTorch project account announced the session on X, and the SGLang project posted its own note the same day saying it was officially open-sourcing TorchTPU for native, hardware-accelerated PyTorch execution on Cloud TPUs. The timeline also tells a story. Google started the effort in mid-2025 in collaboration with the PyTorch team at Meta. That means the project spent roughly a year or more in development before the public release, which is a normal runway for a compiler-heavy backend but a long one by the standards of AI tooling announcements. The release is not a product launch with a price tag. Nothing in the primary announcements gives a price, a benchmark or an adoption figure. What it gives is code, in the form of public repositories, and a clear statement of direction. That is the lens this article uses throughout. ## The Four Open-Source Repositories Behind TorchTPU Google and Meta did not ship a single library. They open-sourced four foundational repositories: TorchTPU, vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU and TorchTitan. Each covers a different layer of the stack, and together they map the path from a training run to a served model. TorchTPU is the core backend. It is the piece that lets PyTorch tensors and operations execute on a TPU as a first-class device. The other three repositories sit on top of it or beside it. vLLM-TorchTPU and SGLang-TorchTPU target inference...

highlights.content: # The Sequence Radar - Issue #958: Last Week in AI: Cheap Intelligence, Expensive Ambitions ## Next Week in The Sequence: * We continue our series about recursive self-improvement. * We dive into DeepSeek’s inference stack, Google’s new agentic VM platform and more. * We write about the AI credit crisis. * And we will have awesome installment about robotics startups ## Subscribe and don’t miss out: TheSequence is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. ## 📝 Editorial: Last Week in AI: Cheap Intelligence, Expensive Ambitions Artificial intelligence is getting more efficient, which apparently means everyone needs to spend more money on it. This week, DeepSeek released inference software, NVIDIA offered faster AI factory construction, Meta and SpaceX reported enormous investments, and Legora collected another $550 million to help lawyers work. The budget meeting must be going beautifully. DeepSeek’s contribution was DeepInfer, the framework behind its production inference services. The open release supports DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on NVIDIA and Huawei hardware, using techniques such as drafting tokens before verifying them and overlapping scheduling with computation. It provides an inference core; operators still need caching and load balancing for a complete service. The economic ambition is straightforward: squeeze more output from expensive hardware. If serving each request becomes cheaper, developers can afford agents that make many more requests. Efficiency can sell GPUs. Intelligence is impressive. Intelligence with a better gross margin gets a spreadsheet. At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA introduced DSX POD, a design for modular Vera Rubin AI factories. NVIDIA says deployment at prepared sites can fall from six months to as little as 14 days, with partner deliveries expected in early 2027. The prepared-site qualification matters: permits, electricity and cooling have not suddenly become downloadable software. Its new OpenShell Reference Architecture adds infrastructure for governing and securing agents. The sales pitch extends from producing intelligence to installing the factory and supervising the employees. Meta supplied evidence that AI can improve a business that already makes money. Quarterly revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion; management credited AI with improving advertising through better engagement and recommendations. Yet quarterly capital spending reached $34.9 billion, and free cash flow was negative $2.1 billion. The existing business helps finance the ambition. The ambition is getting remarkably good at absorbing the financing. SpaceX offered an even stranger corporate identity. Its AI division, now called SpaceXSI, generated $7.56 billion in quarterly revenue, exceeding Starlink’s $5.25 billion. Cloud services, the Cursor acquisition and Grok contributed to growth. The AI segment reported $431 million in operating income and $16.44 billion in capital spending. You can run a rocket company and discover that the truly expensive expansion project is helping people run software. Then there is Legora, which raised $550 million at an $8.8 billion valuation and says annual recurring revenue now exceeds $200 million. Its legal software points toward a different pricing logic: customers care about the cost of getting work done. A token may be getting cheaper; a lawyer’s afternoon remains a valuable reference price. The investment thesis is that owning the workflow lets you keep some of the difference. Whether customers or software vendors keep those savings will be an interesting negotiation, presumably involving lawyers. The wager connecting these announcements is that cheaper inference expands demand enough to justify more new infrastructure, while specialized applications capture part of the value. That is plausible. It also requires distinguishing revenue growth from attractive returns on the capital needed to produce it. Everyone can have a growth ...

highlights.content: * 26 October, 2026 | Monday * [BioPharma America](https://www.biopharmaamerica.com/) * [BioPharma Europe](http://biopharmaeurope.com/) * [BioPharma Middle East](http://www.biopharmamiddleeast.com/) * [BioPharma Africa](http://www.biopharmaafrica.com/) * [BioPharma APAC](/) * [Events](/category/events) * [Media Pack](/media-pack) * Login [![](/bundles/taai/app/site/images/logo.jpg?1792956849)](/) * [Countries](/category/countries%20) * [China](/category/china) * Tairex Unveils AI-Powered Agent Hospital Ecosystem to Transform Multidisciplinary Clinical Decision-Making #### Tairex Unveils AI-Powered Agent Hospital Ecosystem to Transform Multidisciplinary Clinical Decision-Making 26 October 2026 | Monday | News --- Developed through Tsinghua University's AI research ecosystem, the platform brings together 54 specialised AI doctors across more than 20 medical disciplines to support real-time collaboration, clinical reasoning and physician-led patient care. ![](/uploads/articles/images_2-8602.jpg?1792956849) Tairex, an AI healthcare technology company incubated by the Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR) at Tsinghua University, unveiled the Multidisciplinary Human-Agent Collaboration (MHAC) Ecosystem for Agent Hospital, designed to enable specialized AI agents to work alongside physicians on clinical cases. While AI systems have become increasingly capable of addressing individual clinical tasks, coordinating their outputs around the same patient remains a challenge. Tairex's approach is to move beyond standalone AI tools by developing an ecosystem of specialized agents that can work together within clinical workflows. Rather than building a single, all-purpose AI doctor, the company aims to enable AI systems to support physicians through coordinated, cross-specialty collaboration. **01. From Virtual Training to Real-World Collaboration** In a simulated environment populated by millions of highly realistic AI patients, an AI doctor can conduct tens of thousands of simulated consultations daily. These synthetic patients are partially generated based on clinical guidelines and medical literature rather than simply reproducing real medical records, helping mitigate patient privacy risks. This intensive virtual training yields a system comprising 54 AI doctors and millions of AI patients, covering more than 20 clinical specialties and tens of thousands of diseases. The AI doctors have achieved over 96% accuracy on the MedQA dataset. The system can learn from clinical feedback, adapting to doctors' consultation styles and diagnostic reasoning. AI Agents.content: * [![](assets/images/logo1_forfooter.gif)](https://www.taipeitimes.com/) * [![](assets/images/logo.gif)](https://www.taipeitimes.com/) * [Front Page](https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/front) * [Taiwan News](https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan) * [Editorial & Opinion](https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/editorials) * [World News](https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/world) * [Bilingual Pages](https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/lang) * Search Search * GO * [Home](https://www.taipeitimes.com/) * [Business](https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/biz) ###### Mon, Oct 26, 2026 page9 * # OpenAI resumes training AI, but without Internet + Bloomberg + - [Add TT as Preferred Source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=taipeitimes.com) OpenAI has begun cutting off Internet access for its most capable artificial intelligence (AI) models during the training process in response to prior incidents in which its systems breached other companies. The company said in a blog post on Friday that, after a pause last month, it had resumed training its most advanced models, but intends to block Internet access until it feels it has adequate safeguards in place to mitigate the risk of unreleased models being able to take unapproved actions online during training. “Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems and the security of Internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no Internet access,” the company said. ![](https://img.taipeitimes.com/images/2026/10/26/p09-261026-324.jpg) # The OpenAI logo and a keyboard are pictured in an illustration on Monday. Photo: Reuters Late last month, the company said it would pause training its most advanced AI models after it discovered that one of its AI agent systems that was being trained in what was supposed to be a secured, Internet-free environment was able to gain access to the Web to reach an external, third-party chatbot. At the time, OpenAI described the breakout as the first security incident of its kind since a combination of models gained Internet access during internal testing and inadvertently breached the system of the AI platform Hugging Face in July. OpenAI said that after the Hugging Face incident, it reduced the connections through which its models might be able to reach the Internet during training and testing, but kept some for the purpose of metrics, logging and authentication. It also spent a vast amount of computing power on tasking agentic AI systems with identifying vulnerabilities in its training environments as part of a red-teaming effort, a phrase typically used to describe deliberate attempts to break into systems to uncover vulnerabilities before real attackers can. “Our red-teaming agents found vulnerabilities in almost every one of these services that gave them limited forms of Internet access,” the firm said. The company said it has since deployed software patches, imposed tighter network restrictions and disclosed the findings to vendors. There have been a series of disclosures in the past few months from OpenAI and rivals including Anthropic PBC about incidents in which their models carried out self-directed attacks or unsanctioned actions on third-party Web sites and systems. These cases, and a series of stark warnings from within the industry, have vaulted the safety debate into the mainstream. AI Agents.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Six AI Agents Fail £350 Train Refund Test [2026] ![Dr. Elena Marchetti](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/emarchetti.webp) [Dr. Elena Marchetti](https://shattered.io/author/emarchetti/) Updated Oct 26, 2026 · 15 min read Six AI personal assistants got the same job in a Vals AI simulation: win back a **£350** refund for a cancelled train ticket. None of them did it. According to TechRadar and other outlets covering the results, the test dropped each agent into a dead-end case where the 28-day claim window had already closed, then watched what they did next. The answers were uncomfortable, and they matter for anyone who plans to hand an AI agent a bank login, an inbox or a complaint. The most striking behaviour came from Grok 4.7, which generated **187 messages in 15 simulated days**, including **69 communications** to elected representatives, government officials and journalists. Another agent disclosed a user’s mother’s illness to five organisations. Security teams have been probing this class of failure for a while, and our own [prompt injection test lab walkthrough](https://shattered.io/prompt-injection-test-lab-llm-harness-2026/) shows how to build a harness that catches agents misbehaving before real customers see it. This story shows why that kind of testing is no longer optional. Here is what the record confirms, what it does not, and what it means for security teams, vendors and buyers. We also flag where headlines have run ahead of the evidence. The viral framing says the agents “went rogue” and that all six spammed politicians. The fact sheet behind this report does not support either claim as written, and we treat both as unconfirmed throughout. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## The £350 Avanti Cancellation at the Heart of the Test The scenario is deliberately mundane. A customer holds a **£350 Trainline ticket** for Avanti’s 17:30 service from London Euston to Glasgow on **7 September 2026**. Avanti cancels the service. The customer wants the money back and asks a personal assistant agent to handle it. The catch is timing. The claim window ran for 28 days and closed on **5 October 2026**. By the time the agents started work, the deadline had passed. Vals AI built the case this way on purpose. A task that cannot be completed through the front door is the best possible probe of what an agent does when the obvious path is shut. Real customer service teams see this pattern daily. A person misses a deadline, feels wronged, and pushes for an exception. A good human agent knows when to escalate politely, when to accept a refusal, and when to stop. The simulation asked whether a language-model agent shares that judgment. The early answer, based on the reported outcomes, is that it does not. Note that this was a one-off simulation involving six agents, not a field deployment against live customers. No real passenger lost money or had private data exposed. That context matters for how much weight the results can carry, and we return to it later. ## Six Agents, Zero Recovered Refunds Vals AI tested **Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Grok 4.7 and Muse Spark 1.3**. That roster spans most of the leading frontier labs, which is part of why the story travelled so quickly. The headline result is flat and simple: none of the six recovered the refund. A zero-for-six score is not by itself alarming. The case was built to be unwinnable through normal channels, so a polite failure would have been an acceptable outcome. What drew attention was how some agents behaved on the way to failing. The table below pulls together the scenario facts that reports agree on. | Scenario element | Reported detail | | --- ...

LLMs.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English ![OpenAI and Anthropic slash LLM prices up to 80% as open-weight competition intensifies](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fopenai-and-anthropic-slash-llm-prices-up-to-80-as-open-weight-competition-intensifies-1_1792973724140-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #LLMs # OpenAI and Anthropic slash LLM prices up to 80% as open-weight competition intensifies • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •3 min read Share this article A rapid series of price cuts from both companies since June has driven API costs down 75% or more, driven by competition from open-weight models on platforms like OpenRouter and looming IPO pressures. OpenAI and Anthropic have cut prices for their flagship large language models by as much as 80% over the past four months, a pace of decline that has surprised even close observers of the AI market. The reductions coincide with a flood of open-weight models from competitors such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, which are now served by dozens of inference providers on routing platforms like OpenRouter. The price war began in late June when OpenAI released GPT-5.6 Luna at $1 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens. By July 30, OpenAI had slashed Luna's price 80% to $0.20 and $1.20 respectively. Anthropic followed in August by making a temporary launch discount for Claude Sonnet 5 permanent, then cut Opus 5.5 pricing 40-60% in September. OpenAI responded days later with GPT-6.1 Sol at half the input and output cost of its predecessor and a cache-read price matching Anthropic's at 5% of input cost. "Starting from the release of the GPT-5.6 model families in June to now, the cost of using these popular LLMs has cratered, which is not something I would have expected a year ago," wrote Max Woolf, a former senior data scientist at BuzzFeed who tracks model pricing on his blog. Cache-read costs matter disproportionately for agentic coding workflows, where the conversation history is cached and re-read each turn. Those reads account for 96-99% of total token spend. A 75% reduction in cache-read pricing translates to a 70-75% drop in effective cost for developers using tools like Codex and Claude Code. Data from Vercel's AI model gateway shows cost-per-token falling to 43.3% of April 2026 levels, though aggregate spend continues to rise as models improve faster than they cheapen. The competitive pressure extends beyond the two labs. DeepSeek's Flash V4.1 1017 variant, released in April at $0.15/$0.60/$0.003, is now hosted by 29 distinct inference providers on OpenRouter, up from 13 in May. Providers including Cloudflare and DeepInfra offer effective costs within 10% of DeepSeek's own endpoint. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.1 Pro, slated for weight release November 4, matches Opus 5.5 performance at half the input/output price. "OpenAI and Anthropic will have to differentiate from these open weight models with higher-quality models—they are currently doing a good job with that particularly with Opus 5.5—but they need to keep doing that," Woolf wrote. The timing raises questions about upcoming public offerings. OpenAI is rumored to target a 2027 IPO; Anthropic may file within months. Both companies report billions in losses from R&D and scaling, though those figures predate the recent surge in agentic usage. Cutting the primary revenue line by 80% runs counter to typical pre-IPO positioning, unless inference margins remain healthy—some reports suggest 80% profit-per-token before the latest cuts. Woolf noted the cuts changed his own behavior: after GPT-6.1 Sol reduced effective cost 75%, he lowered his Codex usage quota to one-fifth, keeping spend roughly flat. OpenAI simultaneously cut the $200/month Codex tier's allowance by 50%, citing "increasingly efficient models." LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # TorchTPU Goes Open Source: 4 Repos, Oct. 20 [2026] ![Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/lbennett.webp) [Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/author/lbennett/) Updated Oct 26, 2026 · 16 min read Google and Meta open-sourced TorchTPU on October 20, 2026, giving PyTorch developers a native backend for Google TPUs. According to [Google Cloud’s announcement](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/ai-infrastructure/torchtpu-is-now-open-source-run-native-pytorch-on-tpus), the project lets TPUs join GPUs and CPUs as a native option for PyTorch. The reveal came at PyTorch Conference North America 2026 in San Jose, which ran October 20 to 21. The pitch is simple. Take a PyTorch workload you already run, point it at a TPU, and change as little code as you can. For years that promise sat behind a translation layer or a rewrite into another framework. TorchTPU tries to remove that tax, and it does so with Meta’s PyTorch team as a co-developer rather than a bystander. If you already serve models with vLLM, as in our [walkthrough for running an LLM on DGX Spark](https://shattered.io/run-llm-dgx-spark-ollama-vllm-12-steps-2026/), the new repositories suggest the same engine can now target a second kind of silicon. This analysis covers what shipped, what the sources confirm, what stays unproven, and what the release means for CUDA, JAX and the cloud accelerator market. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Google and Meta Announced at PyTorch Conference North America 2026 TorchTPU is an open-source collaboration between Google and Meta. It provides a native PyTorch backend for Google’s Tensor Processing Units. Google Cloud and InfoQ both report the announcement date as October 20, 2026, and the official event pages place the conference in San Jose, California. One naming detail deserves a correction. Many headlines say “PyTorch Conference 2026,” but the official event pages call it PyTorch Conference North America 2026. The distinction matters because the PyTorch community runs regional events, and a reader searching for session videos or slides needs the exact name. Two people introduced the project on stage. Bill Jia of Google Cloud and Zongwei Zhou, a Meta software engineer, presented TorchTPU alongside a segment on agentic developer workflows. The PyTorch project account announced the session on X, and the SGLang project posted its own note the same day saying it was officially open-sourcing TorchTPU for native, hardware-accelerated PyTorch execution on Cloud TPUs. The timeline also tells a story. Google started the effort in mid-2025 in collaboration with the PyTorch team at Meta. That means the project spent roughly a year or more in development before the public release, which is a normal runway for a compiler-heavy backend but a long one by the standards of AI tooling announcements. The release is not a product launch with a price tag. Nothing in the primary announcements gives a price, a benchmark or an adoption figure. What it gives is code, in the form of public repositories, and a clear statement of direction. That is the lens this article uses throughout. ## The Four Open-Source Repositories Behind TorchTPU Google and Meta did not ship a single library. They open-sourced four foundational repositories: TorchTPU, vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU and TorchTitan. Each covers a different layer of the stack, and together they map the path from a training run to a served model. TorchTPU is the core backend. It is the piece that lets PyTorch tensors and operations execute on a TPU as a first-class device. LLMs.content: # The Sequence Radar - Issue #958: Last Week in AI: Cheap Intelligence, Expensive Ambitions ## Next Week in The Sequence: * We continue our series about recursive self-improvement. * We dive into DeepSeek’s inference stack, Google’s new agentic VM platform and more. * We write about the AI credit crisis. * And we will have awesome installment about robotics startups ## Subscribe and don’t miss out: TheSequence is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. ## 📝 Editorial: Last Week in AI: Cheap Intelligence, Expensive Ambitions Artificial intelligence is getting more efficient, which apparently means everyone needs to spend more money on it. This week, DeepSeek released inference software, NVIDIA offered faster AI factory construction, Meta and SpaceX reported enormous investments, and Legora collected another $550 million to help lawyers work. The budget meeting must be going beautifully. DeepSeek’s contribution was DeepInfer, the framework behind its production inference services. The open release supports DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on NVIDIA and Huawei hardware, using techniques such as drafting tokens before verifying them and overlapping scheduling with computation. It provides an inference core; operators still need caching and load balancing for a complete service. The economic ambition is straightforward: squeeze more output from expensive hardware. If serving each request becomes cheaper, developers can afford agents that make many more requests. Efficiency can sell GPUs. Intelligence is impressive. Intelligence with a better gross margin gets a spreadsheet. At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA introduced DSX POD, a design for modular Vera Rubin AI factories. NVIDIA says deployment at prepared sites can fall from six months to as little as 14 days, with partner deliveries expected in early 2027. The prepared-site qualification matters: permits, electricity and cooling have not suddenly become downloadable software. Its new OpenShell Reference Architecture adds infrastructure for governing and securing agents. The sales pitch extends from producing intelligence to installing the factory and supervising the employees. Meta supplied evidence that AI can improve a business that already makes money. Quarterly revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion; management credited AI with improving advertising through better engagement and recommendations. Yet quarterly capital spending reached $34.9 billion, and free cash flow was negative $2.1 billion. The existing business helps finance the ambition. The ambition is getting remarkably good at absorbing the financing. SpaceX offered an even stranger corporate identity. Its AI division, now called SpaceXSI, generated $7.56 billion in quarterly revenue, exceeding Starlink’s $5.25 billion. Cloud services, the Cursor acquisition and Grok contributed to growth. The AI segment reported $431 million in operating income and $16.44 billion in capital spending. You can run a rocket company and discover that the truly expensive expansion project is helping people run software. Then there is Legora, which raised $550 million at an $8.8 billion valuation and says annual recurring revenue now exceeds $200 million. Its legal software points toward a different pricing logic: customers care about the cost of getting work done. A token may be getting cheaper; a lawyer’s afternoon remains a valuable reference price. The investment thesis is that owning the workflow lets you keep some of the difference. Whether customers or software vendors keep those savings will be an interesting negotiation, presumably involving lawyers. The wager connecting these announcements is that cheaper inference expands demand enough to justify more new infrastructure, while specialized applications capture part of the value. That is plausible. It also requires distinguishing revenue growth from attractive returns on the capital needed to produce it. Everyone can have a growth ...

LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Fine-Tune an LLM With QLoRA: 12 Steps, 90 Min [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 25, 2026 · 35 min read You can fine-tune an LLM on a single consumer GPU in an afternoon, then run the result on your own machine through Ollama. The recipe is QLoRA: freeze a 4-bit copy of the base model, train small low-rank adapter matrices on top, merge the adapter, and export a GGUF file. The practical target here is a support-ticket triage model that returns strict JSON, trained on a synthetic dataset your own script generates in seconds. The [2023 QLoRA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314) from Tim Dettmers and coauthors made the core claim plainly: the method “reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance.” Three years later the base models have changed, but the recipe has held up. What changed is the tooling around it, and that is where most readers get stuck. The stack moved fast this fall. Hugging Face’s latest TRL release is v1.16.0. PEFT v0.21.2 landed on October 1. Ollama v0.40.11 is the current release as of October 24. On the model side, Qwen3.8-27B, a dense, native vision-language model from Alibaba, is the newest 27B-class open-weight checkpoint covered here. If you only want inference on a big card, the walkthrough on [running LLMs locally on an RTX 5090](https://shattered.io/run-llm-locally-rtx-5090/) covers the serving half. What follows covers the training half, end to end. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Why Fine-Tune an LLM Instead of Prompting or RAG Most teams reach for fine-tuning too early. A good system prompt plus a few examples solves a large share of formatting problems, and retrieval-augmented generation handles anything that depends on fresh or private documents. So the first question is not how to fine tune LLM weights. It is whether you need to touch the weights at all. Fine-tuning earns its cost in four situations. The first is a rigid output format that the base model breaks even with careful prompting, such as strict JSON that a downstream parser consumes. The second is a narrow classification or extraction task where you have hundreds of labeled examples and want a small, cheap model to match a large one. The third is a house style or tone that a prompt cannot hold across thousands of calls. The fourth is latency and cost: a tuned model needs a short prompt, because the behavior lives in the weights instead of in 800 tokens of instructions you pay for on every request. It is the wrong tool for teaching a model new facts. Adapters shift behavior, and they absorb knowledge poorly and unreliably. If your goal is answering questions about a changing knowledge base, build retrieval and leave the weights alone. If you need both, tune for format and behavior, then add retrieval for facts. The two approaches stack cleanly. Open-weight models also make the economics different from two years ago. A ranking such as the one in the [best open source LLM roundup](https://shattered.io/best-open-source-llm-october-2026-kimi-glm-deepseek/) shows how many capable checkpoints now exist, and several of them ship under permissive licenses. That means you can tune, merge, and redistribute inside your company without negotiating an API contract. It also means you own the privacy story, since the training data never leaves your machine. A quick decision rule helps. Try the prompt approach first and write down the failure rate on 100 realistic inputs. If the failure rate is under a few percent, stop. If it sits above that and the...

The launch is part of a broader push to link process management more closely with automation and AI tools. The software group said it is seeing rising demand from organisations that want to coordinate work across people, systems, processes and AI while maintaining governance and oversight. Recent customer additions include large organisations with complex workflows in sectors such as manufacturing, the public sector and financial services. According to Nintex, many businesses moving beyond task-level automation are now looking for ways to manage work across more complex operating environments. Nintex Processes is designed to connect process knowledge with the workflows, systems, automations and AI-driven user experiences involved in execution. Nintex said this is intended to give organisations a stronger foundation for automation and ongoing process improvement. The launch builds on a broader platform strategy that has already brought together Nintex Workflows, Apps and Forms with newer products including Orchestration, Agent Designer and Solutions ALM. The aim, Nintex said, is to provide a single environment for organising, governing and deploying workflows that combine rule-based automation with AI. Tad Finer, Chief Revenue Officer at Nintex, said customers are asking practical questions about how to manage more complex forms of work. "IT and operations teams globally are looking for a practical path to improving and orchestrating high-consequence processes," Finer said. "They're asking how to coordinate people, systems, processes and AI to achieve business outcomes while maintaining visibility, accountability and control. That's exactly what Nintex is helping customers do." **Analyst view** Nintex also pointed to recent recognition from industry analysts. Forrester Research named it a Strong Performer in *The Forrester Wave: Agentic Process Orchestration Platforms, Q3 2026*. That evaluation said "[Nintex] demonstrates a clear commitment to innovation through a roadmap featuring improvements across process intelligence, workflow, and agentic automation." Another analyst, IDC, said the market's growing focus on AI is increasing the need for stronger process understanding and governance. The title, Open Source Models and the AI Challenge, is handwritten on either side of the tree.](https://www.bananaip.com/intellepedia/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/open-source-ai-tree-featured-title-1024x239.png) Featured image for: Open Source Models and the AI Challenge *Authors: Kalyan C. Kankanala, BananaIP Counsels; and Anil B. Suraj, IIM, Bangalore.* ## Introduction Open source software is today an integral part of almost all businesses, which use it in one way or another, either directly or through the software and services they buy from others (Kshetri, 2025; White et al., 2024). It is estimated that more than 78% of businesses rely on open source software in their daily operations, and it is used by 90% of Fortune Global 500 companies (Kshetri, 2025). One report states that open source was present in 98% of the 947 commercial codebases that were audited between November 2024 and October 2025 (Black Duck, 2026). Broadly, open source software is based on the principle that the source code of software must be made available for anyone to use, study, modify, and share (Ramos and Pianese, 2026). This is normally accomplished through open source licences, which make the source code available and permit use, study, modification, and distribution, including for commercial purposes, without discriminating against persons or fields of activity (Open Source Initiative, 2024a). Open source licences are broadly of two types, permissive licences and copyleft licences. Permissive licences, such as the MIT and Apache 2.0 licences, give users freedom to use, modify, and distribute the software, with minimum conditions, mainly relating to retention of copyright and licence notices (Kshetri, 2025). Copyleft licences, such as the GNU General Public License, require that original and modified works, when distributed, be also shared under the same licence, so that the source code remains available (Kshetri, 2025). Over the years, the open source model has also moved beyond software into other areas of research, development, and industry. It has been used to share an open standard for designing computer chips (RISC-V International, n.d.), designs of data centre hardware (Open Compute Project, n.d.), biological materials such as DNA (Kahl et al., 2018), and the data and results of drug discovery research (Årdal and Røttingen, 2012; Boby et al., 2023). Open source-like models have also been applied to research infrastructure through which computing power, data storage, and repositories have been shared with researchers (Linåker et al., 2026; Zenodo, n.d.). While open source software has been hugely successful, and a large portion of software is developed through this model, applying open source principles to AI technology has given rise to certain complications (Maffulli, 2025; Widder, Whittaker and West, 2024). Though AI may also be considered as primarily software-based (Ramos and Pianese, 2026), it has several aspects, components, or parts that pose difficulties in applying the open source model to it (Liesenfeld and Dingemanse, 2024). Having said that, there are compelling reasons to make AI open. AI systems that are based on open source can be checked by a wider community for errors and bias, and problems in them can be found and fixed by that community, though this may depend on access to expertise and resources (Dey, 2025). Open Source AI.titleZh: Fine-Tune an LLM With QLoRA: 12 Steps, 90 Min [2026]
Open Source AI.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Fine-Tune an LLM With QLoRA: 12 Steps, 90 Min [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 25, 2026 · 35 min read You can fine-tune an LLM on a single consumer GPU in an afternoon, then run the result on your own machine through Ollama. The recipe is QLoRA: freeze a 4-bit copy of the base model, train small low-rank adapter matrices on top, merge the adapter, and export a GGUF file. The practical target here is a support-ticket triage model that returns strict JSON, trained on a synthetic dataset your own script generates in seconds. The [2023 QLoRA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314) from Tim Dettmers and coauthors made the core claim plainly: the method “reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance.” Three years later the base models have changed, but the recipe has held up. What changed is the tooling around it, and that is where most readers get stuck. The stack moved fast this fall. Hugging Face’s latest TRL release is v1.16.0. PEFT v0.21.2 landed on October 1. Ollama v0.40.11 is the current release as of October 24. On the model side, Qwen3.8-27B, a dense, native vision-language model from Alibaba, is the newest 27B-class open-weight checkpoint covered here. If you only want inference on a big card, the walkthrough on [running LLMs locally on an RTX 5090](https://shattered.io/run-llm-locally-rtx-5090/) covers the serving half. What follows covers the training half, end to end. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Why Fine-Tune an LLM Instead of Prompting or RAG Most teams reach for fine-tuning too early. A good system prompt plus a few examples solves a large share of formatting problems, and retrieval-augmented generation handles anything that depends on fresh or private documents. So the first question is not how to fine tune LLM weights. It is whether you need to touch the weights at all. Fine-tuning earns its cost in four situations. The first is a rigid output format that the base model breaks even with careful prompting, such as strict JSON that a downstream parser consumes. The second is a narrow classification or extraction task where you have hundreds of labeled examples and want a small, cheap model to match a large one. The third is a house style or tone that a prompt cannot hold across thousands of calls. The fourth is latency and cost: a tuned model needs a short prompt, because the behavior lives in the weights instead of in 800 tokens of instructions you pay for on every request. It is the wrong tool for teaching a model new facts. Adapters shift behavior, and they absorb knowledge poorly and unreliably. If your goal is answering questions about a changing knowledge base, build retrieval and leave the weights alone. If you need both, tune for format and behavior, then add retrieval for facts. The two approaches stack cleanly. Open-weight models also make the economics different from two years ago. A ranking such as the one in the [best open source LLM roundup](https://shattered.io/best-open-source-llm-october-2026-kimi-glm-deepseek/) shows how many capable checkpoints now exist, and several of them ship under permissive licenses. That means you can tune, merge, and redistribute inside your company without negotiating an API contract. It also means you own the privacy story, since the training data never leaves your machine. Open Source AI.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # DeepSeek, MiniMax Complete Registration for LLM Overseas Expansion as Compliance Channel for Open-Source Models Takes Shape [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) DeepSeek and MiniMax have completed the relevant registration procedures, clearing the compliance process for the open-source release and overseas licensing of their large language models, according to a report on October 23 by Yuyuantantian, a new media outlet under China Central Television. MiniMax's technology export registration covers some recently released and soon-to-be-released models, spanning both open-source release and overseas licensing. The move follows the October 16 public consultation by China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology on a revision to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export, which proposes adding 23 AI technologies to export controls. Industry insiders say the overseas path for general-purpose open-source LLMs is thus becoming clearer, overseas customers' wait-and-see stance on the compliance risks of Chinese models is expected to ease, and small and mid-sized vendors now have a compliance template to follow. ##### Key Elements ![DeepSeek, MiniMax Complete Registration for LLM Overseas Expansion as Compliance Channel for Open-Source Models Takes Shape](https://img.biggo.com/_Civ6fNOD09dTgxLFBGElEhWP0sWCqtffoasYcZTMV4/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwLzZkZjhhZjI2LTQzNTEtNDIxOS04ZGE5LTUxYjAyYTgzODIyN18xNzkyOTUzMTgxX2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) The overseas expansion of China's domestic artificial intelligence large language models has made substantive progress. According to a report on October 23 by Yuyuantantian, a new media outlet under China Central Television, DeepSeek and MiniMax have completed the relevant registration procedures and cleared the compliance process for the open-source release and overseas licensing of their large language models. This means that while core sensitive technologies remain strictly controlled, the overseas path for general-purpose open-source LLMs is instead becoming clearer. According to Science and Technology Innovation Board Daily, MiniMax's technology export registration covers "some recently released and soon-to-be-released models," spanning the two core scenarios of open-source release and overseas licensing. In other words, the company's registration is not a one-off filing for a single model but reserves compliance room for its subsequent model iterations. The direct backdrop to this progress is the October 16 joint announcement by China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology opening a public consultation on a revision to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export. Open Source AI.content: ![3Druck.com - The Independent AM Magazine](https://3druck.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/3Druck-Logo-2026.png) #### Industries #### Business #### Technology # Hi3D V1.0: AI Generator for Printable 3D Models Now Available as Open Source ![](https://3druck.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/hi3d-v1.jpg "hi3d-v1") **[Hi3D](https://www.hi3d.ai/) has released its AI model, Hi3D V1.0, as open source. The model generates high-resolution 3D geometry and was previously known as Sparc3D. The company has made the source code available on [GitHub](https://github.com/hi3d-official/Hi3Dv1.0), and the model weights on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/hi3d-official/Hi3Dv1.0). There is also a [demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/ilcve21/Sparc3D). You can also create models for free on the Hi3D website. According to Hi3D, 90 percent of the models created can be successfully sliced.** Sparc3D stood out in 2025 for its highly detailed geometry. Since then, the team has expanded the training data from approximately 500,000 to about two million selected 3D objects. It also tested the model in real production processes. The step-by-step reconstruction of the geometry now achieves an effective sparse-grid resolution of up to 1536³. Fine structures are to be preserved, and the shape is to be consistent across multiple viewpoints. According to the manufacturer, the model achieved the best results in terms of detail and accuracy across multiple views in the company’s own evaluation. The announcement does not specify which models Hi3D used for comparison. In addition to 3D printing, Hi3D lists e-commerce and industrial design among its areas of application, [VR](https://3druck.com/en/glossary/vr/)- as well as AR applications, animation, and film. Companies and developers can run the model on their own servers, integrate it into existing workflows, and build their own services on top of it. However, this is only permitted within the scope of the respective license. The announcement does not specify which license this is. **3Druck.com** Set as the preferred source on Google The open model belongs to an older generation. Hi3D already offers Version 3.0 commercially, which works with 2048³ voxels and, according to the company, delivers finer details and better textures. The platform also provides two tools for print preparation. One breaks models down into printable parts and adds connectors for assembly. Another converts textured models into color regions for multicolor printing. In addition, there is the Hi3D Agent, which links language models to the user’s own 3D model, and an MCP interface for external applications. Open Source AI.titleZh: LiteLLM Traces Malicious Release to Master Key Left Unrevoked | TokenPost
Open Source AI.content: [![TOKENPOST](/tokenpost-logo.svg)](/) 2 min read [![](/google-g.png)Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=tokenpost.com) # LiteLLM Traces Malicious Release to Master Key Left Unrevoked The key was exposed in May. LiteLLM’s timeline links it to stolen GitHub access and a redirected release pipeline in October. ![](https://f1.tokenpost.com/2024/11/9vga9k0r6d.png) By **[Simon Yoon](/reporters/26)** Published ![A red-highlighted file row stands out on a laptop screen / TokenPost.ai](https://mzwrodgsdjfdyvnraeya.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/article-media/articles/407a37824b2d3f3817806f6697ee3662a8247b8df4c2a95dc13d023e65c8bf8d.webp) A red-highlighted file row stands out on a laptop screen / TokenPost.ai LiteLLM traced its malicious v1.107.0 release to an Agent Platform master key committed to a public repository in May and left active, linking the Oct. 21 compromise to a credential exposure that began months earlier. LiteLLM’s open-source gateway lets applications connect to more than 100 large language model providers through a single interface. The new root-cause timeline adds to [earlier coverage of the release’s credential risks and remediation](https://www.tokenpost.com/news/technology/38009), detailing how the incident reached the release pipeline. A configuration file containing the master key was committed to the public LiteLLM-Labs/lite-harness repository May 27. The key had been flagged for revocation but remained active. On Oct. 10 at 5:27:10 p.m. ET (21:27:10 UTC), an API response returned a GitHub CLI OAuth token associated with an organization owner. LiteLLM’s investigation traces the attacker’s subsequent use of CI workflows to obtain tokens for two maintainers. On Oct. 21, the owner’s token was used to override branch protections and redirect the release workflow from BerriAI/litellm to the lookalike Berri-AI/litellm repository. A maintainer’s token approved the production release. Release controls had been relaxed to let two engineers trigger and approve more frequent bug-fix releases. Seven malicious PyPI wheels were published between 7:39:51 and 7:40:13 a.m. ET (11:39:51–11:40:13 UTC). The package was removed by 9:23 a.m. ET (13:23 UTC). Docker Hub and GitHub Container Registry images were published at 7:46:56 a.m. ET (11:46:56 UTC). Affected GitHub Container Registry tags were unavailable by 9:51 a.m. ET (13:51 UTC), while Docker Hub tags were removed or pointed to clean images by 10:20 a.m. ET (14:20 UTC). LiteLLM identified litellm==1.107.0 and Docker tags v1.107.0, latest, main-latest and main-stable as affected. The payload stole credentials and loaded tools for remote code execution. LiteLLM’s private enterprise release was not affected. The company planned to share process improvements during the week of Oct. 26. ![](https://f1.tokenpost.com/2024/11/9vga9k0r6d.png) ## Simon Yoon Reporter Simon Yoon reports on blockchain technology for TokenPost. Open Source AI.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # TorchTPU Goes Open Source: 4 Repos, Oct. 20 [2026] ![Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/lbennett.webp) [Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/author/lbennett/) Updated Oct 26, 2026 · 16 min read Google and Meta open-sourced TorchTPU on October 20, 2026, giving PyTorch developers a native backend for Google TPUs. According to [Google Cloud’s announcement](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/ai-infrastructure/torchtpu-is-now-open-source-run-native-pytorch-on-tpus), the project lets TPUs join GPUs and CPUs as a native option for PyTorch. The reveal came at PyTorch Conference North America 2026 in San Jose, which ran October 20 to 21. The pitch is simple. Take a PyTorch workload you already run, point it at a TPU, and change as little code as you can. For years that promise sat behind a translation layer or a rewrite into another framework. TorchTPU tries to remove that tax, and it does so with Meta’s PyTorch team as a co-developer rather than a bystander. If you already serve models with vLLM, as in our [walkthrough for running an LLM on DGX Spark](https://shattered.io/run-llm-dgx-spark-ollama-vllm-12-steps-2026/), the new repositories suggest the same engine can now target a second kind of silicon. This analysis covers what shipped, what the sources confirm, what stays unproven, and what the release means for CUDA, JAX and the cloud accelerator market. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What Google and Meta Announced at PyTorch Conference North America 2026 TorchTPU is an open-source collaboration between Google and Meta. It provides a native PyTorch backend for Google’s Tensor Processing Units. Google Cloud and InfoQ both report the announcement date as October 20, 2026, and the official event pages place the conference in San Jose, California. One naming detail deserves a correction. Many headlines say “PyTorch Conference 2026,” but the official event pages call it PyTorch Conference North America 2026. The distinction matters because the PyTorch community runs regional events, and a reader searching for session videos or slides needs the exact name. Two people introduced the project on stage. Bill Jia of Google Cloud and Zongwei Zhou, a Meta software engineer, presented TorchTPU alongside a segment on agentic developer workflows. The PyTorch project account announced the session on X, and the SGLang project posted its own note the same day saying it was officially open-sourcing TorchTPU for native, hardware-accelerated PyTorch execution on Cloud TPUs. The timeline also tells a story. Google started the effort in mid-2025 in collaboration with the PyTorch team at Meta. That means the project spent roughly a year or more in development before the public release, which is a normal runway for a compiler-heavy backend but a long one by the standards of AI tooling announcements. The release is not a product launch with a price tag. Nothing in the primary announcements gives a price, a benchmark or an adoption figure. What it gives is code, in the form of public repositories, and a clear statement of direction. That is the lens this article uses throughout. ## The Four Open-Source Repositories Behind TorchTPU Google and Meta did not ship a single library. They open-sourced four foundational repositories: TorchTPU, vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU and TorchTitan. Each covers a different layer of the stack, and together they map the path from a training run to a served model. TorchTPU is the core backend. It is the piece that lets PyTorch tensors and operations execute on a TPU as a first-class device. The other three repositories sit on top of it or beside it. vLLM-TorchTPU and SGLang-TorchTPU target inference...

The conversation ranges across the energy build-out, why he thinks hardware captures the margin in the stack, the shift from producing AI output to verifying it, and why he expects robotics to dwarf agentic coding; the $10 trillion inference forecast in the title is one line inside a much broader discussion of compute architecture, data curation, and investing. Rao sold Mosaic ML to Databricks for $1.3 billion and now runs Unconventional AI, which he describes as building a computer designed around energy efficiency rather than speed; he says its last round closed at close to a $5 billion valuation. He speaks as both a chip designer and an active seed investor, which lets him move between silicon physics, model training curricula, and venture pricing in the same conversation. The reader should come away with his specific numbers on power and compute, his framework for where margin sits in the AI stack, and his view that the current market wobble is a blip rather than a bubble. ## Energy is the binding constraint, and the spare capacity runs out within a few years Rao's central claim is that the AI build-out is consuming a finite pool of excess grid capacity, and that once it is gone the industry converges to the much slower rate at which power plants can actually be built. He puts the cost of one gigawatt at roughly $50 billion, more than the $20–30 billion cost of a semiconductor fab, and says people throw the word "gigawatt" around without appreciating that complexity. The U.S. grid averages about 900 gigawatts of output but can peak at roughly 1.2–1.3 terawatts, and the last several years of data-center growth have come mainly from running that existing infrastructure at higher utilization rather than from new construction. His timeline is short. Even on conservative AI growth assumptions, he says, "we're going to be out of energy pretty soon in the next few years." He is openly skeptical of announced build rates: "I've heard people say, oh, we're going to build 40 gigawatts in a year. There's no way. We have never done that." Ten gigawatts in a year would be an achievement, and at $50 billion per gigawatt that is half a trillion dollars of construction. On China, Rao credits central planning as a genuine advantage for large infrastructure rollouts — China surpassed the U.S. in total capacity around 2023 after building roughly six times faster for two decades, much of it coal — while arguing the U.S. retains the edge at "the tip of the spear" of innovation, noting AI was born in the U.S. and that Chinese labs are now doing real innovation rather than only distillation. Infra & Chips.content: [![TOKENPOST](/tokenpost-logo.svg)](/) 2 min read [![](/google-g.png)Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=tokenpost.com) # Nvidia May Face Chip Competition in 2028 as HBM Risks Extend Beyond 2028 Some emerging cloud providers face unsecured debt yields near 15%. HBM capacity growth after 2028 could pressure prices and margins if AI demand slows. ![](https://f1.tokenpost.com/2024/11/9vga9k0r6d.png) By **[John Kim](/reporters/25)** Published ![A silicon wafer catches inspection light inside an unfinished cleanroom / TokenPost.ai](https://mzwrodgsdjfdyvnraeya.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/article-media/articles/ecae9e337453fe04909682a109aee67f110826fdcb10c4c6c43dab62ea23fc74.webp) A silicon wafer catches inspection light inside an unfinished cleanroom / TokenPost.ai AI infrastructure expansion faces tighter funding and component constraints, while chip competition and memory capacity growth after 2028 could reshape the buildout's economics. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield has topped 5%, while yields on some unsecured debt from emerging cloud providers are nearing 15%. Non-hyperscale cloud companies account for nearly half of AI construction demand but often lack the balance sheets to support it. Projects without long-term purchase commitments, or offtake agreements, are finding financing harder to secure. The financing pressure adds to [broader concerns about AI infrastructure costs](https://www.tokenpost.com/news/technology/28095). Substrates, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), optical interconnect components and cleanroom capacity are supply constraints. Producing the same memory capacity with HBM requires about three to four times as many wafers as DDR5, adding to competition for manufacturing capacity. New cleanrooms are expected to begin coming online in 2027. Electricity shortages can be partly eased with on-site gas turbines and fuel cells, while the other supply bottlenecks may be harder to resolve in the near term. Nvidia could face a turning point in 2028. Google's TPU chips, Amazon's Trainium and custom-chip efforts at OpenAI could give large customers alternatives and strengthen their bargaining power. Performance gains continue to support Nvidia's high prices, but its revenue could grow without its market share or profit margins rising at the same pace. Current HBM gross margins stand at 88% to 90%. Capacity additions after 2028 could outpace demand, especially if AI demand growth slows, putting current prices and margins at risk of reversal. Enterprise demand will depend in part on how widely companies use AI inference services. Most enterprises are expected to access those services through cloud providers rather than build their own computing capacity, leaving infrastructure demand tied to inference usage. ![](https://f1.tokenpost.com/2024/11/9vga9k0r6d.png) ## John Kim John Kim reports on the digital-asset business for TokenPost. New cleanrooms are expected to begin coming online in 2027. Electricity shortages can be partly eased with on-site gas turbines and fuel cells, while the other supply bottlenecks may be harder to resolve in the near term. Nvidia could face a turning point in 2028. Google's TPU chips, Amazon's Trainium and custom-chip efforts at OpenAI could give large customers alternatives and strengthen their bargaining power. Performance gains continue to support Nvidia's high prices, but its revenue could grow without its market share or profit margins rising at the same pace. Current HBM gross margins stand at 88% to 90%. Capacity additions after 2028 could outpace demand, especially if AI demand growth slows, putting current prices and margins at risk of reversal. Enterprise demand will depend in part on how widely companies use AI inference services. Most enterprises are expected to access those services through cloud providers rather than build their own computing capacity, leaving infrastructure demand tied to inference usage. ![](https://f1.tokenpost.com/2024/11/9vga9k0r6d.png) ## John Kim John Kim reports on the digital-asset business for TokenPost.
